title: Printing And The Accumulation Of Knowledge
text:
Ask what the printing press changed, and the usual answer is that books became cheaper. That is true, but far too small a claim. Movable metal type, developed in fifteenth-century Europe, altered the conditions under which knowledge could accumulate.

Consider what came before it. A manuscript was copied by hand, and every copy introduced fresh errors, so texts tended to degrade as they passed down the generations. Printing reversed that tendency. A corrected edition could be reproduced identically in thousands of copies, which meant a scholar in one city and a scholar in another could argue about the same page of the same book. Standardised diagrams, tables and page numbers made exact reference possible for the first time. The consequences reached well beyond scholarship. Printing in local languages rather than Latin helped standardise those languages and widened the reading public. Religious controversy spread faster than the authorities could suppress it, and practical manuals put technical knowledge into the hands of craftsmen. None of this happened overnight, and manuscripts went on circulating for generations. But the direction is clear: the press turned error from something that accumulated with every copy into something that could be found, corrected and then fixed in place.
points: Cheaper books is the usual answer, but the deeper change was in how knowledge accumulated.
Hand copying introduced new errors with every copy, so texts degraded over time.
Printing produced identical copies, so distant scholars could refer to the same text and page.
Standardised diagrams, tables and page numbers made precise reference possible.
Printing in local languages standardised them, widened readership, spread controversy and circulated practical manuals.
The change was gradual, and manuscripts continued, but errors could now be corrected once and fixed.
